claims.text: A pulsed-laser, low-energy additive-manufacturing regime with active helium gas-jet cooling will reduce residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing.
The proposed regime will improve the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi miniature components relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing.
The intervention uses laser pulse energies of 50–150 mJ and pulse durations below 10 µs.
An active helium gas jet will accelerate heat extraction during printing.
The applicable scan-speed window is 100–300 mm/s.
The proposed processing window applies to miniature components having features below 10 mm.
The intervention will produce a refined, nanostructured, fine-grained cellular microstructure.
The intervention will minimize deleterious phase segregation.
Pulsed laser melting combined with active cooling drastically reduces overall thermal input.
Pulsed laser melting combined with active cooling drastically reduces thermal gradients.
Reduced thermal input and gradients produce ultra-short melt-pool lifetimes.
Ultra-short melt-pool lifetimes limit grain growth.
Ultra-short melt-pool lifetimes limit phase segregation.
Locking in a more uniform, fine-grained microstructure reduces residual stresses.
Locking in a more uniform, fine-grained microstructure enhances mechanical properties.
Intervention-produced components will exhibit improved ductility and strength in tensile and fatigue testing.
Conventional continuous-wave, high-thermal-load additive manufacturing typically produces higher residual stresses.
Conventional continuous-wave, high-thermal-load additive manufacturing typically produces coarser microstructures.
Conventional continuous-wave, high-thermal-load additive manufacturing typically produces degraded mechanical properties.
The hypothesis has not established applicability to larger parts or other alloy systems.
